Every day, Mfon Ndanyongmong’s children ask her the same question: “Mummy, when are we going back home?”
Her family’s home at Ifa Ikot Akpabio, Shelter Afrique Extension, Uyo, the Akwa Ibom State capital, has been overwhelmed by floodwater. Her car remains in the compound, where she says it is sinking into the ground, while her family has been forced to live in a hotel.
What should be the comfort of home has become a place she cannot reach.
“I have passed through severe loss, emotional stress, mental trauma,” Ms Ndanyongmong told PREMIUM TIMES, tears dripping from her eyes.
She said the situation became unbearable on 22 September when officials of the National Emergency Management Agency visited the community and ordered residents to evacuate.
That day, she said, the water rose to her waist as she navigated her compound with her husband and three children to safety.

“It breaks my heart that every day my kids ask me, ‘Mummy, when are we going back home?’ And I do not have an answer to that question,” she said.
Her family is among those affected by severe flooding at Ifa Ikot Akpabio, near Professor Nse Essien Avenue and Grace Land School in Shelter Afrique Extension, an upscale residential estate in Uyo.
Five households have been forced to abandon their homes, according to residents, while other families, particularly those living in storey buildings, remain in the flooded area because they have nowhere else to go.
PREMIUM TIMES visited the community and observed that the floodwater remained too high for the newspaper to access the affected homes. Because of the water level and associated risks, the newspaper could not independently assess the full extent of the damage inside the compounds.
Residents blamed the disaster on an abandoned road construction project, incomplete drainage channels and the concentration of runoff water from adjoining streets in their low-lying neighbourhood.
However, the state environmental protection agency said the affected area was historically a brook and that some buildings might have been constructed on a natural waterway.
The competing accounts raise questions about building approvals, urban planning, drainage design, the supervision of public infrastructure projects and the government’s response to residents who say they have repeatedly sought help.
Residents said the state government awarded the construction of the road to Blagadat Construction Limited, but the contractor abandoned the project around October 2025.
PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify the contractor’s engagement or the circumstances surrounding the reported abandonment. The road had no visible project signboard identifying the contractor, and the state government had not responded to enquiries about the project at the time of publication.
During its visit, PREMIUM TIMES observed that drainage channels constructed along the road connected with drains from other streets but terminated abruptly about halfway along the flooded street.
Residents said the unfinished drainage works had left the area receiving water from adjoining roads without an adequate outlet.
They identified runoff from Rev. Amaowo Road, constructed by Hensek Construction Company, and other adjoining streets as major contributors to the flooding.
They said that the problem went beyond the volume of rainfall to how water from several directions was channelled into their neighbourhood.
Ms Ndanyongmong said drainage channels from four directions now converge on the area, which she described as lower than its surroundings.
She said the drains along Professor Nse Essien Avenue and Rev. Amaowo Road did not discharge adequately into a suitable outlet, leaving water to accumulate in the community.
“After the attempt at road construction, drainage on both sides were done, but it stopped halfway,” she said.
“All the waters from neighbouring communities coming into Shelter Afrique Extension drain into this point. And this point happens to be low.”
She said the flooding had also affected the household water supply. “In my compound, if you turn on the tap from the borehole, you see dirty water. Our soakaway has been filled with water,” she said.
PREMIUM TIMES could not independently prove the precise engineering cause of the flooding or determine whether the drainage designs were approved, properly executed or subsequently altered.
The Ministry of Works had not responded to questions about the project by the time of publication.
The Chairman of the Akwa Ibom State Environmental Protection and Waste Management Agency, Prince Ikim when contacted by PREMIUM TIMES, said the government sympathised with the affected residents but argued that the flooding was not necessarily caused by clogged or inadequate drains.
He said the government had established an Emergency Flood Response Committee headed by the Deputy Governor to address such situations.
According to Mr Ikim, after the flooding at Ifa Ikot Akpabio came to the committee’s attention, members met and delegated a team, including himself, to inspect the affected location.
“Some of the flooding that we see is not caused by clogged drainage. Some are caused by building on waterways. This particular location used to be a brook. Unfortunately, they went and built there. Most of the water is coming from the ground,” he said.
He said the government’s efforts to remove the water had included deploying a fire service truck to pump it out, but the exercise did not produce the expected result.
Mr Ikim said the team’s technical findings suggested that resolving the problem might require demolishing some structures to provide an outlet for the water.
“But who will be willing to allow his building to be sacrificed?” he asked, describing demolition as one of the options necessary to address the situation.
When PREMIUM TIMES told him that residents insisted they had obtained government approval before building their houses, Mr Ikim said he did not know whether such approvals had been granted.
He acknowledged hearing residents’ argument that water from adjoining streets, combined with the abandoned drainage project, had worsened the flooding.
However, he maintained that the affected location was one of the two lowest points in Shelter Afrique, and that its natural terrain had been recognised in the estate’s design. “When there was no development there, because of the natural terrain of it being a brook, water was usually channelled to that point. It served as a natural waterway,” he said.
He added that some buildings in the area appeared to have concrete foundations suggesting their owners knew the area was waterlogged. “We sympathise with them. But this is no fault of the government,” he said.
Mr Ikim said the emergency committee hoped to meet again to consider ways to address the situation. Asked when residents could expect intervention, he said it would happen “soon” but did not provide a specific date.
The agency did not provide PREMIUM TIMES with the technical assessment, drainage plans or other documents supporting its account of the area’s historical status.
When PREMIUM TIMES put the agency’s position to affected residents, they disputed the suggestion that they had built their homes without the necessary government approvals.
Each of the residents contacted by the newspaper insisted that they had obtained the required approvals and that no government agency had stopped them from building at the location.
Charles Ndanyongmong questioned why the government had not publicly make known that the area was a brook where construction should not take place.
“Where has it been gazetted that the area is a brook and no one should build?” he asked.
He also questioned why the government had approved and commenced a road construction project in the area if it was unsuitable for development.
Another resident, Shedrach Mattias, said residents had obtained government approvals before constructing their houses.
“In an estate and urban area like ours, would any reasonable person build without approval?” he asked.
Mr Mattias said he was particularly disappointed that residents had not received what they considered meaningful government assistance despite the prolonged flooding.
He disputed the claim that the government had attempted an emergency relief, saying residents had paid for the interventions, including the fire service’s attempt to pump out the water.
He said he contacted the Ministry of Environment and was told that the government would wait until the dry season before intervening.
“But how do we cope without relief until the dry season?” he asked.
PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify the residents’ building approvals or prove whether the relevant authorities had designated the affected location as a natural waterway before the houses were built.
The newspaper’s enquiries on 26 October to the government sought clarification on the approvals, the drainage infrastructure and the emergency response, but the relevant officials had not provided the requested documents or a detailed explanation by the time of publication.
The conflicting accounts leave key questions unanswered: whether the houses were approved, whether the drainage design adequately accounted for the area’s terrain, and whether the reported road project has worsened the situation.
For Dennis Hanson, the flooding has changed an ordinary residential street into a place where leaving home has become a struggle.
He said he first noticed unusual flooding in July. At the time, residents could still move around, although they sometimes had to fold their trousers or drive through high water to leave the area.
The situation deteriorated in September, when water began flowing into the street from adjoining roads, alongside water channelled through the drainage channels.
Mr Hanson, who lives with a family of six, said they were still trying to manage life in the area despite damage to property and disruption to their daily activities.
For other families, remaining in their homes has become impossible.
Grace Shedrach said she had been unable to access her house and that the belongings inside had been lost to the flooding. Her dog, she said, remained trapped on the property.
“It has been a horrible experience. I don’t even know whether my dog is still alive,” she said, blaming the abandoned road project and the absence of a proper drainage outlet.
She said affected residents had pooled their resources to find a solution, but their efforts had not substantially reduced the water.
“The money we spend for about five weeks now to stay in the hotel with family is too much. We want to return home,” she said.
The prolonged displacement has disrupted children’s schooling and imposed additional costs on families who must pay for accommodation while their homes remain inaccessible.
Ms Ndanyongmong said preparing her child for school from a hotel had become particularly distressing.
She has lived in the community for 12 years and said she had never witnessed flooding on this scale.
Before turning to the government for help, residents said they attempted to tackle the flooding themselves.
Ms Ndanyongmong said affected households pooled resources to purchase sandbags, use tarpaulins to barricade their gates and hire pumping equipment to remove the water.
They also engaged a geologist and bought pipes to channel the water away from their properties.
Residents said they invited the State Fire Service to pump out the water, but the available equipment and tanker were too small to make a meaningful difference.
They said their efforts were overwhelmed by the volume of water entering the neighbourhood.
“Intervention would need government effort, not individuals or community effort,” Mr Hanson said.
The residents have also submitted formal requests for government intervention.
PREMIUM TIMES sighted a letter received by the Ministry of Works on 5 October from one of the affected households. Another letter, addressed to the Office of the Deputy Governor, was received on 6 October.
In the letter to the Ministry of Works, the resident described how drainage from Rev. Amaowo Road and the abandoned road project had allegedly concentrated water in the area without a proper discharge point.
The resident appealed for the immediate deployment of a high-capacity pumping machine to evacuate the floodwater through a temporary hose to a suitable underground drainage system.
The letter also requested that the construction company be directed to return to the site and complete the abandoned road and drainage works.
However, when PREMIUM TIMES visited the community on 26 October, the floodwater remained high and some households were still displaced.
Residents said no government agency had visited the community to assess their situation following the flooding and their formal appeals, apart from the fire service intervention they said they had funded.
The affected area is also only a few poles from the residence of the Secretary to the State Government, Enobong Uwah. Residents said they had made repeated attempts to draw the authorities’ attention to their plight.
The flooding has brought to the fore questions about the implementation of Akwa Ibom’s public spending plans for flood control, particularly as successive state budgets have provided billions of naira for drainage infrastructure.
A review of the 2026 approved budget shows that the state allocated N1.5 billion under the Ministry of Works for the construction of the 6.1-kilometre Shelter Afrique/Nung Ette Flood Control Tunnel in Uyo Local Government Area.
The project received a budgetary allocation of N500 million in 2024 and N2 billion in 2025 .
The allocations raise questions about the project’s implementation status, the amounts actually released and spent, and whether the planned infrastructure has reached the stage where it can protect vulnerable communities.
A budgetary allocation does not show that the money has been released, spent or translated into completed infrastructure.
PREMIUM TIMES on 26 October sought information from the Ministry of Works on the project’s status and expenditure, as well as the measures planned to address the flooding at Ifa Ikot Akpabio.
The newspaper also asked whether the ministry assessed the drainage designs and discharge points of adjoining roads before approving the works, whether it awarded the reported abandoned road project, what explains the contractor’s alleged abandonment of the site and when work would resume.
The Commissioner for Works, Eno Ibanga, did not respond to calls from PREMIUM TIMES. A formal media enquiry sent to the commissioner was also not responded to at the time of filing the report.
The state budget contains other provisions intended to support emergency response and flood management.
The Office of the Deputy Governor received a budgetary provision of N9.3 million for the purchase of equipment for emergency services.
The Akwa Ibom State Infrastructure and Assets Management and Maintenance Agency was allocated N3 million for first-aid kits, emergency alarms and response equipment.
The Ministry of Science and Digital Economy also received N10 million for a security-reporting application through which citizens could report crimes and make emergency calls.
Separately, the Akwa Ibom State Environmental Protection Agency was allocated N2.5 billion for drainage, canal desilting and flood control in Uyo metropolis and its environs.
These provisions make the implementation of the state’s flood-control plans and its response to residents’ complaints matters of public accountability.
The residents have not limited their appeals to formal letters.
On 3 October, Ms Ndanyongmong published a Facebook post about the flooding under the name Mfon Essien. The post, which received 98 shares, tagged the verified Facebook page of Governor Umo Eno, the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) and the South South Development Commission.
Victor Antai, the NDDC’s Executive Director of Projects, also has a residential building in the estate, according to information provided to PREMIUM TIMES.
The residents’ appeals have also drawn attention to the role of ecological funding in addressing environmental challenges in the Niger Delta.
A review of Federation Account Allocation Committee disbursements reports cited by our reporter indicates that 50 per cent of ecological funds accruing to states and local governments in the Niger Delta is deducted at source for the NDDC. This raises queries about how ecological resources intended for the region are deployed to address persistent environmental risks.
Many commenters on Ms Ndanyongmong’s post tagged the governor, official Akwa Ibom State Government accounts and other prominent political figures, calling for intervention.
On 22 and 27 October , further posts on the flooding prompted further appeals from the public for government assistance.
Yet residents said they were still struggling to pay for temporary accommodation after five weeks away from their homes.
PREMIUM TIMES contacted the Commissioner for Information, Aniekan Umanah on Monday to obtain the state government’s response to the flooding. A call to Mr Umanah was rejected, and a media enquiry sent to him had not received a response by the time of publication.
The newspaper also contacted the Press Secretary to the Deputy Governor, Omen Bassey on Monday.
Mr Bassey initially said he was about to board a flight and should be contacted again. PREMIUM TIMES informed him that it was ready to send a formal media enquiry, which was subsequently shared with him.
When the newspaper called again later in the afternoon, he said he had yet to settle in Abuja and would speak to PREMIUM TIMES later. He had not responded to the enquiry at the time of publication.
The newspaper asked whether the Office of the Deputy Governor had received the residents’ complaint, what action followed, whether an assessment had been conducted and what emergency measures the government would provide to protect affected families.
It also sought clarification on the government’s plans to drain the affected area, restore access to homes and address the underlying causes of the flooding.
The unresolved issue at Ifa Ikot Akpabio follows concerns about the state’s ability to prevent disasters and respond when they occur.
In a May 2026 investigation, PREMIUM TIMES reported that traders at Akpan Andem Market in Uyo suffered devastating losses when a fire broke out and the nearby fire service station could not immediately deploy its truck because of a shortage of diesel.
The investigation also found that a proposed Akwa Ibom disaster risk management and emergency response framework, developed through consultations involving government agencies and other stakeholders, had yet to translate into visible institutional reforms.
The report documented concerns about delayed implementation and the need for a coordinated emergency response system. The Office of the Deputy Governor said the proposed framework was being reviewed against existing laws and that legal advice was being sought.
The flooding at Ifa Ikot Akpabio presents another test of whether emergency planning and public budget provisions can be translated into timely action when residents face immediate danger.
In July, PREMIUM TIMES also reported that flooding affected several Uyo communities, damaging homes and property and prompting residents to protest over delayed road projects and drainage problems. The report examined substantial budgetary allocations for flood control and sought explanations from government officials about the implementation of planned interventions.
The latest incident raises a related call for clarification: what happens when residents report a crisis, submit formal complaints and make public appeals, but remain displaced while the underlying infrastructure problems continues.
The government’s position that the affected area was a natural waterway also raises a separate accountability point of contention. If the location was unsuitable for residential development, what safeguards were in place to prevent construction? If residents obtained the required approvals, why did the government issue them, and what assessments informed those decisions?
Likewise, if the flooding is primarily a consequence of the site’s natural terrain, the government still needs to explain what immediate measures can protect residents and whether the proposed demolition of structures is necessary, proportionate and supported by a documented technical assessment.
Residents of Ifa Ikot Akpabio insist that their immediate priority is the removal of the floodwater, the restoration of safe access to their homes and a credible plan to prevent a recurrence.
They also want the government to show why the water has accumulated in their street, whether the abandoned project contributed to the crisis and which authorities or contractors must take responsibility for resolving it.
Until the water recedes, families such as the Hansons remain caught between the cost of leaving their homes and the risks of staying.
For Ms Ndanyongmong, the most painful consequence is the question she faces every day from her children.
She has no date to give them yet. The government has not provided one.
And as the floodwater continues to occupy the place her family calls home, the question of when they can return remains unanswered.
